variants.title: Gamma attenuation in aluminium
variants.sample: Sealed Cs-137 gamma source with aluminium absorbers
variants.unknown: the attenuation coefficient and half-value thickness of aluminium
variants.note: Aluminium is the usual absorber in a teaching laboratory: its half-value thickness at 662 keV is about 34 mm, so the sheets are thick but easy to handle.

source.title: NIST XCOM / Hubbell mass attenuation tables: aluminium 0.07465 cm2/g at 662 keV, density 2.699 g/cm3, so mu = 0.2015 /cm

variants.title: Gamma attenuation in copper
variants.sample: Sealed Cs-137 gamma source with copper absorbers
variants.unknown: the attenuation coefficient and half-value thickness of copper
variants.note: Copper is three times denser than aluminium and its atoms are heavier, so it halves the beam in about 11 mm instead of 34.

source.title: NIST XCOM / Hubbell mass attenuation tables: copper 0.0730 cm2/g at 662 keV, density 8.96 g/cm3, so mu = 0.654 /cm

variants.title: Gamma attenuation in lead
variants.sample: Sealed Cs-137 gamma source with lead absorbers
variants.unknown: the attenuation coefficient and half-value thickness of lead
variants.note: Lead is the shielding material of a radiation laboratory: at 662 keV it halves the beam in under 5 mm, because photoelectric absorption grows steeply with the atomic number.

source.title: NIST XCOM lead: 0.1248 (600 keV), 0.0887 (800 keV) cm2/g, log-log interpolated to 0.1111 cm2/g at 662 keV; density 11.35 g/cm3
source.note: mu = 0.1111 x 11.35 = 1.260 /cm. Corrected from an earlier 0.1248, which is the 600 keV value. Interpolated from remembered XCOM table points: verify against the NIST XCOM table before relying on it.
